Across town, at Bethel Community Health, the phone started ringing. Bethel was going to become the county's lone hospital, with the nearest emergency room more than an hour away.

Bethel's patient population mirrored the county's socio-political divide. Rural, repeatedly conservative and deeply religious, many of the county's voters faced rising health-care costs while trying to scrape together for their children's college educations. Others lived in affluent cities, many of whose residents were college-educated former Oregonians who'd fled the state's high taxes and crash-and-burn economy. They were people who'd played a role in defeating Measure 3. (Among them were members of Oregon Colleges Coalition, a group of state college presidents that spent $500,000 opposing the levy as it did not raise enough revenue to solve the state's long-term economic crisis.) By defeating the levy, they had helped to create a problem.

Many were social liberals who cared about social justice. They had seen a rural community with no online grocery store but a 7-Eleven on every corner. They had seen when a truck driver was killed a year earlier, when his employers tried to kick him off the company's medical plan. Now they felt alone. There was nowhere for him to get medical care.

"I grew up in the Northwest," says a former college president. "I believed in community, civic responsibility and the government working with everybody toward the common good. Most of my life I felt that was happening. But in this Measure 3 election, it was my perception at least, that Oregon didn't want to be part of that. That we had to take care of ourselves here in the West Hills."

They called Bethel like they called the governor, then secretary of state, and other elected officials. "They were mad as hell," remembers Lynn Higgins, a doctor who led the transition. "Some were infuriated. Some were asking what they could do. What we've all continually been struck by is that nobody wants to see big government coming in and repeating the same disaster we've just had."

After the election she hired me to teach her public speaking. She wanted to learn how to tell her story about why everyone should vote for the ER.

Normally when someone wants to learn public speaking it's because he has a presentation scheduled at Microsoft or Goldman Sachs; he wants to keep his job and agrees to take the class only if it's not called "giving presentations." When you teach a class like that, your room is usually filled with men, or with the woman who usually does the ordering for the company. There's no tests, you get paid to tell your jokes, and the class moves briskly along to the topics those adults imagine are the most useful: how to memorize your points, not shuffle your feet around when you're talking, and what not to eat before you give your speech—onions?—which will make your face smell like that when you talk.

It was uncomfortable the first couple of times I taught Teresa's class. She'd made the conscious decision to vote yes on the levy, which no one she worked with would do, and in her day job most of the folks she encountered were people who had few qualms about slamming the residents of Grant County. She wanted, she said, to talk about why the ER meant so much to her and convince her colleagues to let it stay open. And she wanted me to teach her how to do it without being fired.

"What scares me," she told me, "is that I'm thinking about it and I haven't decided how I'd even open."

Teresa was a nurse, but--as she had always insisted to her family and friends, even before the hospital's financial crisis--her life's calling was as a writer. When she was sixteen she'd started a zine called The Safety Net, whose circulation peaked at a hundred and forty-seven subscribers in eighth grade. It was almost all poetry, but she'd branched out into a serial, "The Demon Nurses' Ball," which was set in Grant County Memorial ER.

For twenty years the notebook in which she'd written remained shut. Then, her fiftieth birthday approaching, she bought a laptop and signed up for a creative-writing class on the campus in Bend. In the first class of the term the instructor asked the students to write about the day they'd been born.

Teresa was the only student who opened her piece with a blood gases printout.

At home she'd set the document beside her bed. The numbers on it weren't that of a newborn baby but of her nephew Andrew, who, at five days old, had been airlifted from the ER in a ride that lasted eight minutes and cost more than a new car. A variety of infections and failures of the lungs--each one named, each one recorded in his chart, like the weather--had conspired until his little body went into septic shock. Though he pulled through, spent weeks in the NICU, and went on to thrive, the bill from that eight-minute ride would dog his parents for more than a decade.

By the time Teresa finished the memoir about Andrew's birth she had written more than twelve thousand words. The next day she submitted it to The Sun Magazine, which accepted it and, a few months later, published it in its winter-2010 issue.

An in- depth study published in 2016 by the New York University School of Medicine cited data showing that the average American's blood-pressure reading rose sharply during the month of the 2012 elections. Even on the morning after Election Day, these blood pressures hadn't returned to normal. Your blood pressure is, of course, just a piece of vital data sent along the highways of your body. Your body's messengers also include hormones, other proteins, immune cells, and a cornucopia of other substances. The more researchers learn about them, the more they see that the kind of stress that comes from reading incessantly about the loss of political ground can truly imperil your health. Being exposed to political squabbles triggers our sympathetic nervous system, telling us to defend ourselves against a threat. And that can be literally threatening to your health; researchers have found that even modest aggravations, from job interviews to traffic jams, can generate changes that affect our cardiovascular system, which is responsible for delivering essential circulating components to all of your organs. That, according to a group of economists and political scientists, is how democracy worked. Voters sent to the ballot issues beyond the comprehension of most voters, and then the ones who cared most — and usually had the most to gain — got out the vote.

"Many of the most consequential issues in the modern democracies are quite complex. Citizens are less informed on some of these huge, consequential decisions than others," said Larry Bartels, a professor of government at Vanderbilt University.

The 2016 presidential election had been an elaborate campaign of persuasion. The Trump campaign promised to install a Republican in the White House against all odds. The Clinton campaign spent more than a billion dollars trying to defeat him.

Local measures went to the ballot a little nearer to neutral. Democrats and Republicans vied for control of a state legislature, a city council, a school board. But on matters that weren't overtly political, voters made decisions without the help of party professionals or their advertising money, and in the absence of the news media's interest. People voted not because they were swayed by an argument put forward by a campaign or a reporter or a celebrity. They voted because they cared.

By design, American democracy forces important decisions to be narrow — both in principle and in practice. A president with legislative majorities can outlaw slavery, or send troops to Cambodia, or launch a preemptive invasion a month before an election. A county council can raise property taxes, or pass new zoning laws, or decide how to regulate vacation rentals.

Nobody can agree exactly how much of a role proximity to the issue plays in how people vote. But this country has always had trouble making collective decisions. It's impossible for a nation of three hundred million people to deliberate in person.

Teresa burst into tears. She'd call in sick tomorrow, she decided. "How can we lose," she wondered, "when our lives are at stake?"

In the end, county voters chose to close Grant County Memorial. Measure 3 failed again in May 2017 and again in November, when it got just 42.4 percent of the vote. At its board meeting twelve days later, the hospital's leadership voted to close the ER on January 2.

Why are small hospitals closing all over rural America? It's a story of demographic inevitability, political ideologies, war over taxes, and — as Teresa discovered — a struggle to draw a connection between a vote and a hospital.

A little over a hundred years ago, Grant was one of the strongest counties in Oregon. In the early 1900s hardy homesteaders began settling here. They dug wells and planted potatoes, lumbered the Ponderosa pines, and raised beef cattle. By the 1920s they were sending train- and truckloads of livestock, timber, and wheat to the rest of the country. Towns like John Day and Canyon City grew into thriving county seats where people came to shop, have fun, and be taken care of when they were sick.

But by the time Teresa was born, in 1968, the way of life here was already falling apart. Factory farming had made industrial-scale agriculture more efficient, putting smaller family farms out of business. Sawmills were being shut down by environmental regulations. Railroad tracks were ripped up. More and more crop and timber industries fell into the hands of multinational corporations, and the profits they generated flowed into the East Coast and abroad.

The small towns that were left had to do more with less. As revenue declined, schools closed, streets went unplowed, and water and sewer systems fell into disrepair.

Grant County Memorial Hospital was built in 1972, after a fire destroyed the previous facility. Over the years its finances ebbed and flowed — with the overall economy, and with changes in the way Medicare and Medicaid reimbursed it. In 2008 it reached a crisis point when it lost its administrator, its surgeon, and two key doctors. All three quit in the summer within a few weeks of each other.

Within Grant County, Canyon City is sometimes called “the city.” More properly, though, it’s the capital of the county, the largest of the six towns, with around 1,000 people, more than twice as many as John Day, the next largest town. All but the smallest towns in Oregon are officially designated as cities by the state, but Canyon City is the smallest (population-wise) of them all.

That population is about what it was a century ago, when the city thrived as both a rural service center and the center of the district’s gold mining. A sign on I-84 calls it the “Gateway to the Wonders of Grant County” and invites you to “come see the real Oregon.”

Founded in 1862, Canyon City is one of the older towns on the high east side of the Cascades, and its historic downtown has a few of the handsome stone buildings that were inevitably built in “the 60s” -- the 1860s. Some, though, are a little more roughly built, and tumble-down too, with tar paper and overgrown weeds where windows and sidewalks should be.

The town is set on the southeast side of the John Day Valley -- the four towns on the opposite side of I-84, clustered around an outlet of the river, are collectively referred to as “John Day” in almost a polite insult. All of Canyon City’s water came from wells until 1997, when the city built a treatment plant up on the north side of town, where I-84 crosses the city’s water basin, Deer Creek. The phrase I've used here is an example of a literary device called analepsis (also called an anachronism or flashback). Analepsis (from the Greek αναληψις, meaning "a taking up again") is a narrative technique in which a scene is inserted in a chronological sequence that interrupts the normal chronological order of the narrative, to fill the reader in on events that occurred before. We use analepsis to give backstory. An analepsis is different from a prolepsis, which is a scene set in the future relative to the current chronological position in the story. We do often use prolepsis for "flashforward."

In this case we've used this analepsis to provide backstory. To dig into that writerly craft, think about the advantages of this approach:

1. The reader gets to see the background events before she knows what happened on election night, instead of getting the backstory after we've established the failure of the measure. This order makes the failure of the measure more impactful because we've seen how much the community and Teresa had tried to make the measure pass.

2. We focus the reader on what matters. This way, the reader sees what the pending closing looks like from a human scale, rather than diving into the failure and then having flashbacks about what happened leading up to this point. The anecdote about Caleb with asthma sets up a personal stake that pulls the reader in.

3. We use the way we set up events to increase the forewarning and suspense of the failure to pass. We show, through tension delivered in short paragraphs, what the pending failure looks like. We break the action up into separate actions, finished with fairly short paragraphs, much the way that present literary action would be. This structure builds tension.
